articles.title: What The Flock: Prison Populists and Palantyranny
articles.author: Pine and Roses -- Maine DSA
articles.content_excerpt: There is a peculiar American humiliation in having to explain why you would like to buy groceries without helping populate a police database. You needed eggs. Apparently, you also owed somebody a record of the trip. Flock Safety’s roadside cameras collect license plates, vehicle characteristics, locations, and timestamps. Pass one and your car can become a searchable observation, available to an investigator with access. The company describes these as snapshots of public vehicle information . Such a modest word, snapshot. A birthday. A beach. Your car passing an intersection while you are trying to get through a Tuesday. A collection of those observations has a different character. articles.title: Saudi Arabia’s Yemen Strategy Has Fallen to Pieces
articles.author: Helen Lackner
articles.content_excerpt: Over the past few weeks, Yemen’s Ansar Allah movement, also known as the Huthis, has launched an offensive and made big territorial gains. The latest turn in the Yemeni civil war could have major implications for the world economy, as it involves one of its most important trade routes through the Red Sea. It certainly poses a big challenge for Yemen’s neighbor Saudi Arabia. Helen Lackner is a leading expert on the politics of Yemen and the author of several books about the country. She spoke to Jacobin about the background to the latest developments and what is likely to happen next. This is an edited transcript from Jacobin’s Long Reads podcast. articles.title: Greed and Economic Desperation Are Fueling Sudan’s Civil War
articles.author: Ahmed Ismat Ahmed
articles.content_excerpt: I used to pass the biscuit factory in Soba without going in. People I knew went in for a twelve-hour shift on a line that smelled of sugar and oil. In 2021, the number that stuck was 1,500 pounds for the shift. In Haj Yousif, where Iqbal lived, the rent for a single room was 30,000 pounds a month. You had to work twenty factory days just to cover rent. Meanwhile, the Rapid Support Forces were offering people 15,000 a day, a uniform, and a phone. Those three numbers explain more about Sudan’s war than any map I have been shown since. What happened in Sudan was not primarily a story of people choosing violence. articles.title: A Union Feud Shouldn’t Sink California’s Billionaire Tax
articles.author: Christie Offenbacher
articles.content_excerpt: America’s already threadbare welfare state is on the brink of total collapse. Over the next ten years, national funding for Medicaid, whose benefits 81 million Americans rely upon, will be cut by about $1 trillion . States that expanded Medicaid access under the Affordable Care Act will be hit especially hard. More immediately, in just a few days, on October 1, and again on January 1, various new requirements for Medicaid eligibility will be instituted. This means that receiving and maintaining insurance will suddenly become much more difficult for millions of Americans. The result of all of these changes, enacted by H. articles.title: The First Walmart Union Contract in North America
articles.author: Kari Thompson
articles.content_excerpt: Eight hundred workers at a Walmart distribution center in Mississauga, Ontario, succeeded where others have not: they are now working under a two-year contract with North America’s largest logistics giant. The landmark collective bargaining agreement went into effect on July 1, nearly two years after workers won union representation , joining Unifor Local 252, motivated by low wages and unsafe working conditions. As punishment two years ago, Walmart bumped the pay of every logistics worker in Canada — except those who unionized. articles.title: AI Destruction Isn’t Hypothetical. It’s Already Here.
articles.author: Branko Marcetic
articles.content_excerpt: We’re several weeks into a fierce debate over whether artificial intelligence (AI) will kill us all. Triggered by a spate of former workers at major AI firms coming forward to warn that a future superintelligent AI could lead to human extinction, the debate has inspired a kaleidoscopic array of views that don’t break down along neat ideological lines. Some think it’s all hogwash, either the product of ignorant hype or part of a cynical hype campaign by the industry itself. For others, convinced that the tech’s potential capabilities are no joke, they’re warnings that need to be taken deadly seriously.In many ways, though, the debate is besides the point.
